common_name: Low Scape Hedger Aronia (Columnar Fruitless Black Chokeberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this naturally narrow, columnar selection needs no shearing to hold its shape.

directions: Low Scape Hedger is a Proven Winners black chokeberry selection bred for a naturally upright, narrow-columnar habit that forms a tidy low hedge or screen without pruning, unlike the spreading habit of the wild species. Clusters of white spring flowers with brick-red anthers open along the branch tips, and glossy dark green summer foliage turns strong orange in fall; unlike fruiting aronia cultivars, this selection does not set berries, keeping the plant clean and low-litter near patios and walkways. It is exceptionally adaptable to heat, cold, wet, and dry soils alike, and thrives in both full sun and the dappled light under high tree canopy. Space plants 2-3 feet apart for a continuous low hedge, and prune immediately after bloom only if a formal shape is desired.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, including dry shade under open tree canopy; Pacific wax myrtle tolerates coastal salt spray and sandy or poor soils once established.

directions: Pacific wax myrtle is a dense, broadleaf evergreen native to coastal bluffs, dunes, and stream banks from Vancouver Island to southern California, forming a large multi-stemmed screening shrub or small tree with glossy, aromatic, spicy-scented leaves. Small waxy purple-black drupes ripen in fall along female plants and are a valued food source for wintering birds, while root nodules fix nitrogen, letting the shrub thrive in the lean, sandy soils typical of its native range. It handles full coastal sun as readily as the partial shade of a woodland edge, and its salt tolerance and dense habit make it one of the best native choices for a living windbreak or privacy screen along the Pacific Coast. Group several plants for a continuous hedge, or let it grow untrimmed into its natural rounded form.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Don's Dwarf Southern Wax Myrtle (Compact Evergreen Bayberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; this compact selection stays far smaller than the wild species, making it usable as a low evergreen hedge.

directions: Don's Dwarf is a compact selection of southern wax myrtle that holds a dense, multi-stemmed form at 4-6 feet, a fraction of the size of the species, which can reach 20 feet unchecked. Grayish-green, aromatic, narrow leaves stay evergreen in mild winters, and abundant blue-gray waxy berries form on female plants from midsummer into fall, feeding wintering songbirds. It tolerates heat, drought, salt spray, and periodically wet soils with equal ease, though foliage can suffer dieback in harsh, windy winters at the cold end of its range. Use it as a low, informal evergreen hedge or foundation planting in partial shade to full sun, and prune lightly after the main flush of spring growth if a tighter form is wanted.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Magical Moonlight Buttonbush (Compact Fragrant Native Wetland Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; excellent for rain gardens and pond margins where a smaller buttonbush is needed than the straight species.

directions: Magical Moonlight is a rounded, mounded buttonbush selection bred to stay at a garden-friendly 5-6 feet, roughly half the size of the wild species, while keeping its signature large, exceptionally fragrant spherical white flower clusters that draw hummingbirds, butterflies, and bees over a long summer bloom season. Fruits that follow are noticeably larger than the species' and persist into fall and winter, feeding waterfowl and songbirds. Like all buttonbush it loves consistently wet or even seasonally flooded soil, making it a natural fit for rain garden basins and pond edges, though it adapts reasonably well to average garden moisture once established. Plant in partial shade to full sun and skip supplemental fertilizer, since this wetland native performs best in lean, damp soil.
sources: University of Kentucky Nursery Crop Extension

common_name: Copper Bush Honeysuckle (Red-Tinted Native Groundcover Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in dry to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Copper tolerates dry shade as readily as the species and spreads slowly by stolons to form a low colony.

directions: Copper is a low, vigorously mounding selection of native bush honeysuckle distinguished by red-tinted stems and new foliage that unfurls in coppery bronze tones before settling to green, then returning to rich red and purple in autumn, giving three seasons of stem and leaf color on a plant otherwise grown mainly for toughness. Small, lemon-yellow tubular flowers appear in summer and are visited by bumblebees, though the foliage color is the main draw. Like the species it spreads slowly by underground stolons into a low colony, making it useful as a colorful, deer-resistant groundcover shrub for dry shaded slopes or the poor soil near building foundations where few other flowering natives perform. Little maintenance is needed beyond an occasional cutback in late winter to encourage the most vivid new copper growth.

common_name: Bobbee Northern Bayberry (Compact Glossy-Leaved Native Bayberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in poor to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Bobbee is a Lake County Nursery selection prized for larger, glossier foliage than the wild species.

directions: Bobbee is a named selection of northern bayberry chosen for foliage that is notably larger, glossier, and more wavy-textured than the species, giving it a more refined look while keeping all the toughness that makes bayberry a go-to plant for difficult coastal and urban sites. Its aromatic, leathery leaves are semi-evergreen to deciduous depending on winter severity, and on female plants clusters of small waxy gray-blue berries persist through winter, providing crucial cold-season food for tree swallows, yellow-rumped warblers, and other birds. Root nodules fix nitrogen, letting it thrive in lean, sandy, or salt-affected soils where few other natives succeed, and it tolerates both full coastal sun and the partial shade of a woodland or dune edge. Use it as an informal hedge, mass planting, or erosion-control shrub, and plant at least one male nearby to ensure fruit set on female specimens.
